title: Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge
titleBreak: Beat the Whites|with the Red Wedge
lede: El Lissitzky’s Civil War poster turns a political slogan into pure geometry: a red triangle drives into a white circle on a black field.
summary: A red wedge pierces a white circle; the slogan runs on diagonals in black, outline, and red capitals. El Lissitzky, Vitebsk, 1919–1920.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the Russian State Library scan published on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Klinom_Krasnym_Bej_Belych.JPG) (3360 × 2688 px, viewed at 1920 px). The Commons record names the Russian State Library as the holding institution and gives no call number.

styles.note: The founding image of the style’s graphic language: red and black on paper, a diagonal wedge, a circle, and rotated block capitals.

context: Lissitzky made the poster during the Russian Civil War, in which the Bolshevik “Reds” fought the anti-Bolshevik “Whites”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_the_Whites_with_the_Red_Wedge).

The imprint at the bottom reads “№ 19 Литиздат. Политуправления Запфронта” (lithographic publishing office of the Political Administration of the Western Front) and “Уновис”, the group around Kazimir Malevich in Vitebsk. The sheet measures 48.8 × 69.2 cm according to the Commons record.

Wikipedia records that the art historian Maria Elena Versari connects the image to Italian Futurism, and that Nikolai Kolli built a “Red Wedge” monument in Moscow in 1918 with the same symbol. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_the_Whites_with_the_Red_Wedge).
observed: The format is landscape. The ground is unprinted cream paper, framed by a thin black rule.

A large red triangle enters from the upper left and points into a white circle that sits on a black field. The black field is cut by a diagonal edge that runs from the top center to the bottom center.
Small red and black splinters, bars, and a gray stippled rectangle scatter around the point of impact.
“КЛИНОМ” runs down to the right in heavy black sans-serif capitals. “КРАСНЫМ” follows in outline capitals on a steeper diagonal.
“БЕЙ” is set in red capitals inside the white circle, and “БЕЛЫХ” is set in outline capitals on a gray stippled block on the black field.
The only hue is an orange-red. Everything else is black, gray tint, and paper.
interpretation: The poster states the style’s whole grammar in one sheet: one hue, a diagonal thrust, elementary shapes that carry the meaning, and words that follow the direction of the shapes instead of a baseline.
The screenshot measurement finds exactly one hue and 9% chromatic area, inside the style’s fingerprint for `color.hues` and `color.chromaticShare`.
borrow: Let one red shape point at the most important element on the page, and make everything else black, gray, or paper.
Rotate each word of a short heading to a different angle so that the words follow the shapes.
Split the ground into a light and a dark field with one diagonal edge.

images.alt: Landscape poster on cream paper: a large red triangle from the upper left points into a white circle set on a black field, with scattered small red and black bars and Russian words in black, outline, and red capitals set on diagonals.
images.caption: El Lissitzky, *Beat the Whites with the Red Wedge*, 1919–1920, lithograph. Russian State Library, image from [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Klinom_Krasnym_Bej_Belych.JPG).

rights.statement: Commons marks the scan {{PD-Art|PD-old-auto-expired}} (Public Domain Mark). Lissitzky died on 30 December 1941. Under Article 1281 of the Russian Civil Code, as summarized in the Commons template PD-Russia-expired, works of authors who died before 1 January 1952 are in the public domain in Russia in 2026, including the four-year extension for authors who worked during the Great Patriotic War. The poster was published before 1931, so it is also in the public domain in the United States.
